title: Vaccines in Pregnancy: A Review of Guidelines
abstract: Abstract Importance: Vaccination during pregnancy protects both the pregnant individual and the fetus from severe infectious diseases. Maternal immunization has expanded over the past decade, with new vaccines, robust safety data, and clear evidence of neonatal benefit through transplacental IgG transfer. Objective: To summarize current evidence regarding the safety, efficacy, and clinical recommendations for vaccines administered before and during pregnancy, outline strategies to address vaccine hesitancy, and provide an updated reference of vaccines recommended and contraindicated during pregnancy. Evidence Acquisition: Evidence synthesized from guidelines issued by the CDC, ACOG, SMFM, and major peer-reviewed publications including randomized trials, observational studies, vaccine safety surveillance systems, and meta-analyses. Literature informing disease burden, immune physiology, and perinatal outcomes associated with vaccine-preventable diseases also reviewed. Results: Influenza, Tdap, and COVID-19 vaccines demonstrate strong maternal and neonatal protective effects with excellent safety profiles. The RSV vaccine offers additional infant protection against severe lower respiratory tract disease. Several other vaccines (e.g., hepatitis A and B, meningococcal, polio, rabies) can be administered in pregnancy when clinically indicated. Live-attenuated vaccines remain contraindicated. Maternal immunization is most effective when integrated into routine prenatal care with onsite availability. Vaccine hesitancy can be mitigated through evidence-based counseling, addressing safety concerns, and improving the provider-patient trust relationship. Conclusion: Maternal immunization is safe, effective, and essential for preventing morbidity and mortality among pregnant individuals and infants. Relevance: This review provides clinicians with an updated guide for counseling, administering, and optimizing vaccine use before, during, and after pregnancy.

Results: Influenza, Tdap, and COVID-19 vaccines demonstrate strong maternal and neonatal protective effects with excellent safety profiles. The RSV vaccine offers additional infant protection against severe lower respiratory tract disease. Several other vaccines (e.g., hepatitis A and B, meningococcal, polio, rabies) can be administered in pregnancy when clinically indicated. Live-attenuated vaccines remain contraindicated. Maternal immunization is most effective when integrated into routine prenatal care with onsite availability. Vaccine hesitancy can be mitigated through evidence-based counseling, addressing safety concerns, and improving the provider-patient trust relationship. Conclusion: Maternal immunization is safe, effective, and essential for preventing morbidity and mortality among pregnant individuals and infants. Relevance: This review provides clinicians with an updated guide for counseling, administering, and optimizing vaccine use before, during, and after pregnancy.

title: Bridging the Knowledge Gap on Rabies: A Cross-Sectional Study of General Practitioners’ Awareness and Clinical Management in Pakistan
abstract: Objective: This study aimed to assess the knowledge regarding rabies and its management among general practitioners in Pakistan.Methods: This cross-sectional study was conducted from March to December 2023 among general practitioners practicing in public and private clinics or hospitals in different cities of Pakistan. Using non-probability convenient sampling technique, a pre-tested structured questionnaires was administered among GPs to assess the knowledge and practices regarding rabies and its management. Descriptive statistics for frequency and percentage were acquired for all variables. Continuous variables are presented as mean ± SD. Independent t-test was used to compare mean knowledge and practice score and its association with demographic variables. Data was analyzed by using SPSS version 24. A P value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.Results: Out of total 500 general practitioners, 258 (51.6%) from public hospitals, and 108 (21.6%) had more than 10 years of experience. The overall mean age of the participants was 36.3 ± 7.8 years. General practitioners, (89.4%) correctly knew about the causative agent and (49.4%) about the vector of rabies. More than half of the general practitioners (53.4%) responded correctly that rabies prevention can be achieved using either cell culture vaccines or nervous tissue vaccines and (66%)had knowledge regarding anti-rabies vaccination schedule. Regarding management of dog bite wound (85.4%) had appropriate knowledge about irrigation and (27.4%) about suturing. Collectively (52%) general practitioners recognized the need to administer antibiotics along with tetanus antitoxin to patients with dog bite. Statistically no significant association was observed between knowledge and practice scores with socio-demographic characteristics.Conclusion: This study revealed that the knowledge of rabies and its management was inadequate among general practitioners of Pakistan. Frequent sessions on awareness and management of dog bite patients should be held for general practitioners to control and reduce the incidence of human rabies related deaths.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to assess the knowledge regarding rabies and its management among general practitioners in Pakistan. Conducted as a cross-sectional study from March to December 2023, it involved 500 GPs from public and private clinics across different cities. Using non-probability convenient sampling, a pre-tested structured questionnaire was administered to evaluate knowledge and practices. The results indicated that 89.4% of participants correctly identified the causative agent of rabies, while only 49.4% recognized the vector. Regarding management, 85.4% had appropriate knowledge about irrigation of dog bite wounds, but only 27.4% knew about suturing. Additionally, 52% of GPs recognized the need to administer antibiotics along with tetanus antitoxin. However, no significant association was found between knowledge and practice scores with socio-demographic characteristics. The study concluded that the knowledge of rabies and its management was inadequate among GPs in Pakistan, highlighting the need for frequent awareness sessions to reduce human rabies-related deaths. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the use of non-probability sampling and the lack of detailed demographic analysis.

title_zh: 弥合 狂犬病 的知识差距:巴基斯坦全科医生意识和临床管理的横断面研究
source_body_en: Objective: This study aimed to assess the knowledge regarding rabies and its management among general practitioners in Pakistan.Methods: This cross-sectional study was conducted from March to December 2023 among general practitioners practicing in public and private clinics or hospitals in different cities of Pakistan. Using non-probability convenient sampling technique, a pre-tested structured questionnaires was administered among GPs to assess the knowledge and practices regarding rabies and its management. Descriptive statistics for frequency and percentage were acquired for all variables. Continuous variables are presented as mean ± SD. Independent t-test was used to compare mean knowledge and practice score and its association with demographic variables. Data was analyzed by using SPSS version 24. A P value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.Results: Out of total 500 general practitioners, 258 (51.6%) from public hospitals, and 108 (21.6%) had more than 10 years of experience. The overall mean age of the participants was 36.3 ± 7.8 years. General practitioners, (89.4%) correctly knew about the causative agent and (49.4%) about the vector of rabies. More than half of the general practitioners (53.4%) responded correctly that rabies prevention can be achieved using either cell culture vaccines or nervous tissue vaccines and (66%)had knowledge regarding anti-rabies vaccination schedule. Regarding management of dog bite wound (85.4%) had appropriate knowledge about irrigation and (27.4%) about suturing. Collectively (52%) general practitioners recognized the need to administer antibiotics along with tetanus antitoxin to patients with dog bite. Statistically no significant association was observed between knowledge and practice scores with socio-demographic characteristics.Conclusion: This study revealed that the knowledge of rabies and its management was inadequate among general practitioners of Pakistan. Frequent sessions on awareness and management of dog bite patients should be held for general practitioners to control and reduce the incidence of human rabies related deaths.
abstract_zh: 目的:本研究旨在评估巴基斯坦全科医生对 狂犬病 及其管理的了解。方法:这项横断面研究于 2023 年 3 月至 12 月在巴基斯坦不同城市的公立和私人诊所或医院执业的全科医生中进行。使用非概率方便抽样技术,在全科医生中进行了预先测试的结构化调查问卷,以评估有关 狂犬病 及其管理的知识和实践。获得所有变量的频率和百分比的描述性统计数据。连续变量以平均值±标准差表示。独立 t 检验用于比较平均知识和实践得分及其与人口统计变量的关联。数据采用SPSS 24版进行分析。P值<0.05被认为有统计学意义。结果:500名全科医生中,258名(51.6%)来自公立医院,108名(21.6%)拥有10年以上经验。参与者的总体平均年龄为 36.3 ± 7.8 岁。全科医生(89.4%)正确了解病原体,(49.4%)正确了解 媒介 或 狂犬病。超过一半的全科医生 (53.4%) 正确回答,可以使用细胞培养物 疫苗 或神经组织 疫苗 来实现 狂犬病 预防,并且 (66%) 了解有关抗 狂犬病 疫苗接种 时间表的知识。关于狗咬伤伤口的处理(85.4%)有适当的冲洗知识和(27.4%)有缝合知识。总体而言(52%)全科医生认识到需要对被狗咬伤的患者使用抗生素和破伤风抗毒素。从统计上看,知识和实践得分与社会人口特征之间没有显着关联。结论:这项研究表明,巴基斯坦全科医生对 狂犬病 及其管理的了解不足。应经常为全科医生举办有关狗咬伤患者的认识和管理的会议,以控制和减少与人类 狂犬病 相关的死亡。

full_text: Abstract Rabies remains a formidable global public health challenge, attributable to viruses of the genus Lyssavirus. Control efforts have progressed markedly through the introduction of inactivated vaccines, rabies immunoglobulin (RIG), and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), which collectively provide both pre- and post-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP and PEP). In low-resource environments, however, PEP implementation is hindered by the lack of highly sensitive diagnostic assays. At present, the gold-standard techniques endorsed by the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) and the World Health Organization (WHO) — namely the Rapid Fluorescent Focus Inhibition Test (RFFIT) and the Fluorescent Antibody Virus Neutralization (FAVN) assay — are employed to quantify rabies virus neutralizing antibody (VNA) titers. These assays, nonetheless, are labor-intensive, time-consuming, and necessitate handling of live virus. This review elucidates emerging methodologies for antibody quantification against rabies virus. Notably, the recent advancement of an Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) — characterized by rapid turnaround, high specificity and sensitivity, cost-effectiveness, and scalability has significantly enhanced detection of antibodies directed against the rabies virus glycoprotein. We also discuss the principle technical obstacles encountered during the assay development. Looking forward, these innovations are poised to improve both the accuracy and throughput of rabies serology, thereby streamlining efficacy evaluations and prophylaxis monitoring, and ultimately bolstering global rabies control and eradication initiatives. full_text_sections.full_text: Abstract Rabies remains a formidable global public health challenge, attributable to viruses of the genus Lyssavirus. Control efforts have progressed markedly through the introduction of inactivated vaccines, rabies immunoglobulin (RIG), and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), which collectively provide both pre- and post-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP and PEP). In low-resource environments, however, PEP implementation is hindered by the lack of highly sensitive diagnostic assays. At present, the gold-standard techniques endorsed by the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) and the World Health Organization (WHO) — namely the Rapid Fluorescent Focus Inhibition Test (RFFIT) and the Fluorescent Antibody Virus Neutralization (FAVN) assay — are employed to quantify rabies virus neutralizing antibody (VNA) titers. These assays, nonetheless, are labor-intensive, time-consuming, and necessitate handling of live virus. This review elucidates emerging methodologies for antibody quantification against rabies virus. Notably, the recent advancement of an Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) — characterized by rapid turnaround, high specificity and sensitivity, cost-effectiveness, and scalability has significantly enhanced detection of antibodies directed against the rabies virus glycoprotein. We also discuss the principle technical obstacles encountered during the assay development. Looking forward, these innovations are poised to improve both the accuracy and throughput of rabies serology, thereby streamlining efficacy evaluations and prophylaxis monitoring, and ultimately bolstering global rabies control and eradication initiatives. title_original: Rabies: a brief note on diagnostics and prophylactics

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study addresses the need for improved diagnostic methods for rabies virus, particularly in low-resource settings where current techniques are limited by their complexity and requirements for live virus handling.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a review of methodologies for rabies virus diagnostics and prophylactics, focusing on human and animal rabies, with an emphasis on vaccine quality control and antibody detection in vaccinated individuals.
analysis.methods: The study discusses the development and validation of ELISA techniques for quantifying rabies virus glycoprotein antibodies, as well as real-time RT-PCR assays for rabies virus quantification in vaccines and the use of metagenomic next-generation sequencing for rabies virus diagnosis in cerebrospinal fluid.
analysis.main_results: The study reports the development of a novel ELISA for measuring glycoprotein in human rabies vaccines and the validation of a real-time RT-PCR assay for rabies virus quantification. It also highlights the use of metagenomic sequencing for rabies virus detection.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret these findings as significant advancements in rabies diagnostics, offering more efficient and scalable methods for antibody detection and virus quantification, which could improve vaccine quality control and serological monitoring.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These innovations can enhance the accuracy and speed of rabies diagnostics, particularly in resource-limited areas, and support better vaccine monitoring and public health initiatives for rabies control.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on a review of existing methodologies and does not present original experimental data, which limits the strength of the evidence. However, it provides a comprehensive overview of current and emerging diagnostic techniques.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores the challenges and advancements in rabies diagnostics and prophylactics, emphasizing the need for improved methods in low-resource settings. It highlights the limitations of traditional assays like RFFIT and FAVN, which are labor-intensive and require live virus handling. The study discusses the development of ELISA techniques for antibody quantification, real-time RT-PCR for virus detection, and metagenomic sequencing for etiological diagnosis. These innovations are interpreted as significant steps toward more accurate and scalable diagnostic tools, which could enhance vaccine quality control and public health initiatives. The findings suggest that these methods may improve rabies serology and monitoring, supporting global rabies control efforts. However, the study is based on a review rather than original data, which limits the strength of the evidence.

Biosensor as an alternative diagnostic method for rabies virus detection: A literature review. Review on Rabies and Vaccines. J Virol Methods [Internet]. A comparative review of serological assays for the detection of rabies virus-specific antibodies. Immunological aspects of rabies: a literature review. Arctic-like lineage of rabies virus detected in Indian wild fox: a case study. Abstract Rabies remains a formidable global public health challenge, attributable to viruses of the genus Lyssavirus. Control efforts have progressed markedly through the introduction of inactivated vaccines, rabies immunoglobulin (RIG), and monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), which collectively provide both pre- and post-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP and PEP). In low-resource environments, however, PEP implementation is hindered by the lack of highly sensitive diagnostic assays. At present, the gold-standard techniques endorsed by the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) and the World Health Organization (WHO) — namely the Rapid Fluorescent Focus Inhibition Test (RFFIT) and the Fluorescent Antibody Virus Neutralization (FAVN) assay — are employed to quantify rabies virus neutralizing antibody (VNA) titers. These assays, nonetheless, are labor-intensive, time-consuming, and necessitate handling of live virus. Notably, the recent advancement of an Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) — characterized by rapid turnaround, high specificity and sensitivity, cost-effectiveness, and scalability has significantly enhanced detection of antibodies directed against the rabies virus glycoprotein.
